name: Alabama
analysis: Alabama's 2019 SB 47 authorizes driverless operation only for automated commercial vehicles, with a $2 million liability minimum, owner-as-operator liability and a bar on AV-specific local or state requirements. It does not create a passenger robotaxi pathway.
oversight: Alabama DOT has state-level jurisdiction under the commercial vehicle framework.

name: Alaska
framework: No enacted AV operation framework identified
analysis: Proposals to restrict autonomous operation and assign operator liability remained under consideration in the 2026 survey. Proposed bills are not current operating authority.
oversight: General motor vehicle law applies while the proposed AV measures remain unenacted.
source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

name: Arizona
analysis: Arizona allows driverless operation under HB 2813 (2021, A.R.S. § 28-9702) once an operator files a law-enforcement interaction plan and a written acknowledgment of federal, traffic, insurance and registration compliance; ADOT can issue a cease-and-desist letter if either is missing. The statute builds on 2015 and 2018 executive orders. A company operating in Arizona does not have statewide service coverage.
oversight: Arizona MVD notification and certification.
source_label: Arizona DOT AV framework and HB 2813 history

name: Arkansas
analysis: Arkansas Act 468 (2019) allows autonomous and fully autonomous vehicles only under a pilot program approved by the State Highway Commission, which is deemed approved 60 days after submission. The program must state its commercial purpose and insurance needs, and no more than three vehicles may operate at once.
oversight: State submission and applicable traffic and vehicle rules.

name: California
analysis: California regulates AVs in two tracks. The DMV (Vehicle Code § 38750, Articles 3.7 and 3.8) issues testing with a driver, driverless testing and deployment permits and collects collision reports; the CPUC separately authorizes passenger service. A DMV permit alone does not authorize paid rides.
oversight: DMV: vehicle testing, deployment permits and reporting. CPUC: passenger service pilots, fare-charging deployment, passenger safety and service reporting.

name: Colorado
framework: AV operating framework; truck restrictions vetoed
analysis: Colorado's SB 17-213 (2017) makes automated-driving-system regulation a statewide concern, bars local standards that differ from those for human drivers, and authorizes systems that can follow every state and federal driving law. A system that cannot must get Colorado State Patrol and CDOT approval before testing.
oversight: State motor vehicle law and any applicable testing conditions.

name: Connecticut
analysis: Connecticut's Public Act 17-69 (2017) is a pilot, not statewide authority: up to four municipalities may host fully autonomous vehicle testing under agreements fixing routes and hours, with at least $5 million in insurance, self-insurance or bond. A task force studies fully autonomous vehicles and the pilot reports annually.
oversight: Pilot approval and participating municipalities.

name: Delaware
framework: No enacted AV-specific operating statute identified
analysis: Delaware's 2025 proposal to require an onboard operator failed. Its AV advisory activity does not itself grant a commercial permit.
oversight: Ordinary vehicle rules; no distinct statewide commercial AV permit identified in the guide.
source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

name: Florida
analysis: Florida Statutes § 316.85 allows driverless operation with no person physically present and treats the automated driving system as the operator. On-demand networks must meet § 627.749 insurance requirements, and local governments may not add taxes, fees or other requirements, though airports and seaports may charge reasonable fees.
oversight: Vehicle registration and statutory operating requirements.

name: Georgia
analysis: Georgia's SB 219 (2017) allows a fully autonomous vehicle to operate with no human driver if it meets federal standards, can reach a minimal-risk condition, is registered as such and has liability coverage meeting the state minimum. Driver licensing does not apply. The statute does not show where any operator actually runs.
oversight: State motor vehicle law and applicable service regulation.

name: Hawaii
analysis: Hawaii Act 21 (2020) is a testing pilot run by the Department of Transportation, allowing testing on public roads only with a human driver physically present to intervene. The department decides which entities may test, and the pilot did not grant general driverless commercial authority.
oversight: Hawaii DOT determined eligible pilot testers.

name: Idaho
analysis: Idaho's executive-order committee examined testing and deployment issues. The 2026 survey identified no enacted AV-specific operating statute.
oversight: General motor vehicle requirements and agency guidance.
source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

name: Illinois
analysis: Illinois Vehicle Code § 11-208(e-10) bars local governments, including home-rule units, from prohibiting automated-driving-system vehicles or regulating them inconsistently with the Vehicle Code, while keeping local traffic control. It is a preemption rule, not a statewide permit or deployment framework.
oversight: State vehicle and traffic law; local powers are constrained by statute.

name: Indiana
framework: No enacted AV-specific operating statute identified
analysis: Indiana's 2025 bill addressing autonomous tractor-trailers failed. The 2026 survey did not identify a dedicated AV operating law.
oversight: Ordinary vehicle and commercial-carrier requirements.
source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

name: Iowa
analysis: Iowa Code §§ 321.514–321.519 (2019 SF 302) authorize driverless-capable vehicles and give the Department of Transportation rulemaking authority. Under the department's rules, Level 4 and 5 vehicles do not need a conventional human driver and registrants must say whether a vehicle is driverless-capable.
oversight: State traffic and vehicle requirements under Iowa's AV statute.

name: Kansas
analysis: Kansas K.S.A. 8-2902 allows driverless-capable vehicles to operate without a human driver if they can reach a minimal-risk condition, follow traffic laws and carry required federal labels, with a law-enforcement interaction plan on file with the Highway Patrol. A human driver must be present for a vehicle's first 12 months in Kansas service, except vehicles not designed for people.
oversight: State vehicle and traffic rules.

name: Kentucky
analysis: Kentucky's HB 7 (2024) creates a fully autonomous vehicle framework administered by the Transportation Cabinet, requiring $1 million in insurance, registration and a law-enforcement interaction plan, with limits on local regulation. Vehicles over 62,000 pounds needed a credentialed human driver until July 31, 2026.
oversight: State vehicle law and any remaining commercial-carrier requirements.

name: Louisiana
analysis: Louisiana R.S. 32:400.3 (Act 232 of 2019) lets autonomous commercial motor vehicles operate with no driver in the vehicle if they meet federal and state requirements and carry at least $2 million in coverage. The authority covers commercial vehicles only, so passenger service cannot be inferred from it.
oversight: State commercial-vehicle and traffic requirements.

name: Maine
analysis: Maine has no driverless-operation statute: Resolve Chapter 46 created a Commission on Autonomous Vehicles and directed the Department of Transportation to set up a process authorizing AV testers to demonstrate and deploy automated driving systems for testing on public ways. The commissioner can halt testing that threatens public safety.
oversight: Maine DOT pilot rules and general vehicle requirements.

name: Maryland
analysis: Maryland Transportation Article §§ 15-901 to 15-903 cover only commercial or industrial vehicles and mainly let autonomous vehicle converters sell or lease aftermarket-converted vehicles without a dealer or manufacturer license. They do not set general rules for driverless operation on public roads.
oversight: Motor Vehicle Administration and applicable vehicle law.

name: Massachusetts
analysis: Executive Order 572 established a testing framework in 2016 and was rescinded by Executive Order 603 in 2022. Current testing authority needs separate verification.
oversight: Do not rely on the rescinded order for current testing.
source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

name: Michigan
analysis: Michigan Vehicle Code § 257.665 allows manufacturers and upfitters of automated driving systems to research and test automated vehicles on public roads, with or without a human operator, after showing insurance and minimal-risk capability. The engaged system counts as the driver, and § 257.665c lets the state designate automated vehicle roadways and preempts conflicting local ordinances.
oversight: State AV statutes and vehicle rules.

name: Minnesota
framework: No comprehensive AV operation law enacted
analysis: Minnesota proposed an AV and on-demand network framework in 2026, but it failed. The proposal should not be represented as an active permit system.
oversight: General vehicle rules and any relevant agency guidance.
source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

name: Mississippi
analysis: Mississippi's MS FAVE Act (HB 1003, 2023, effective July 1, 2023) allows fully autonomous vehicles without a human driver, with proof of financial responsibility, state registration and titling, and a law enforcement interaction plan whose section is written to be repealed July 1, 2026. State agencies and localities may not add AV-specific taxes, fees or requirements.
oversight: State traffic, registration, and safety requirements.

name: Missouri
analysis: A Missouri proposal requiring an active human driver was still pending in the survey. Its introduction alone does not change current AV operating law.
oversight: General state motor vehicle and carrier rules.
source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

name: Montana
analysis: Montana Code § 61-6-409 (2025) allows Level 1–3 automated driving systems on public highways and Level 4–5 vehicles subject to limits set by Department of Transportation rulemaking. Cities may regulate traffic but cannot discriminate against vehicles with automated driving systems.
oversight: State vehicle and commercial-carrier requirements.

name: Nebraska
analysis: Nebraska Revised Statute 60-3302 (LB 989, 2018) permits driverless-capable vehicles on public roads with no human driver if they can reach a minimal risk condition and comply with state traffic law, including at railroad crossings, unless the department grants an exemption.
oversight: State statutory requirements for driverless operation and ordinary vehicle law.

name: Nevada
analysis: Nevada's DMV runs a self-certification system under NRS chapters 482A and 482B: applicants register for testing with bond and insurance, then certify specific make, model and year vehicles for operation. The DMV does not test or certify the technology, and 2011 AB 511 and 2017 AB 69 built the statutory base.
oversight: Nevada DMV testing and operation certification.

name: New Hampshire
framework: Testing pilot and conditional driverless operation
analysis: New Hampshire RSA 242:1 sets up a DMV pilot for testing automated vehicles, with $5 million in financial responsibility and a $500 annual fee, and also allows driverless-capable vehicles and on-demand driverless networks on public roads under conditions on minimal risk, traffic law, federal rules and insurance.
oversight: Pilot approval and commission reporting.

name: New Jersey
analysis: A 2026 bill proposed a fully autonomous vehicle pilot. The guide identifies it as pending, so a proposed pilot cannot be shown as active authorization.
oversight: General motor vehicle rules pending enacted AV legislation.
source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

name: New Mexico
framework: Statute with NMDOT notification and certification rule
analysis: New Mexico regulates AVs under a 2021 statute (HB 270, NMSA 66-7-13) and an NMDOT rule (18.24.1.9 NMAC, April 2022): owners notify NMDOT before public-road testing, vehicles meet federal and traffic law, and fully driverless testing needs a submitted testing statement and certification. Local bans based solely on automation are barred. Later bills adding human-operator requirements (HB 378, HB 148) were not confirmed enacted.
oversight: State transportation and testing-notification requirements.

name: New York
framework: State demonstration permit; additional NYC test permit
analysis: New York has no permanent AV statute; the DMV runs a demonstration and testing permit program that requires a licensed person in the driver's seat, a law enforcement interaction plan and $5 million in insurance, under a law the DMV says expires April 1, 2028. Testing in New York City also needs a separate NYC DOT permit.
oversight: NYS DMV demonstration program; NYC DOT testing permit within the city.
source_label: New York State DMV AV demonstration

name: North Carolina
analysis: North Carolina G.S. 20-400 to 20-402 (2017) lets fully autonomous vehicles operate without a licensed driver if they meet federal standards, can reach a minimal risk condition, are registered as fully autonomous and are insured. The registered owner answers for moving violations and localities cannot regulate these vehicles separately.
oversight: State traffic law and committee-led policy review.

name: North Dakota
analysis: North Dakota Century Code § 39-01-01.2 allows an autonomous vehicle to operate without a human driver if it can reach a minimal risk condition after a system failure and meets registration, title and insurance rules. A person using the vehicle is not driving it and needs no license; existing liability law is unchanged.
oversight: Ordinary vehicle law plus the state's AV operating provision.

name: Ohio
analysis: Ohio's DriveOhio program requires companies to register before AV testing. The guide identifies no general AV operation statute; registration should not be read as commercial deployment approval.
oversight: DriveOhio testing registration and state vehicle rules.
source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

name: Oklahoma
analysis: Oklahoma SB 1541 (2022) allows fully autonomous vehicles without a human driver once a law enforcement interaction plan is filed with the Department of Public Safety and at least $1,000,000 in insurance or self-insurance is shown. On-demand networks follow the Transportation Network Company Service Act.
oversight: State traffic, registration, and on-demand network requirements.

name: Oregon
framework: Task force, no general operating law
analysis: Oregon established an AV task force. A 2026 proposal to permit operation without ordinary driving privileges failed.
oversight: General vehicle law while broader AV operation proposals remain unenacted.
source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

name: Pennsylvania
analysis: Pennsylvania Title 75 Chapter 85 (Acts 117 of 2018 and 130 of 2022) makes PennDOT the lead agency and requires a certificate of compliance based on self-certification before operating highly automated vehicles, with or without a driver. The certificate holder is treated as the driver for violations and local rules are preempted.
oversight: PennDOT self-certification and state traffic requirements.

name: Rhode Island
framework: No dedicated AV operating law identified
analysis: The 2026 survey identifies no AV-specific statute or new proposal. That does not establish that an individual deployment is authorized.
oversight: General motor vehicle and service rules.
source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

name: South Carolina
framework: No dedicated AV operating law identified
analysis: South Carolina's survey entry identifies no new AV legislation since 2018. Operator status still depends on general vehicle law and any service-specific rules.
oversight: General state motor vehicle requirements.
source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

name: South Dakota
analysis: South Dakota HB 1095 (2024) lets fully autonomous vehicles operate with no human driver if the system is engaged and can reach a minimal risk condition and follow traffic law. The system is the driver, violations are imputed to the owner, vehicles must be insured and report their autonomy level, and localities may not add AV-specific rules.
oversight: State AV, commercial-carrier, and traffic rules.

name: Tennessee
analysis: Tennessee's Automated Vehicles Act (Public Chapter 474, 2017) lets ADS-operated vehicles run with no human driver if they meet federal standards, can reach a minimal risk condition and are registered as ADS-operated. Its $5 million insurance requirement was written to sunset July 1, 2021, and political subdivisions may not prohibit or regulate these vehicles.
oversight: State traffic law and the Automated Vehicles Act.

name: Texas
analysis: Texas SB 2205 (2017) authorized driverless operation under Transportation Code ch. 545 subch. J. SB 2807 (2025) made the automated driving system the operator and requires TxDMV authorization for commercial driverless operation, enforceable from May 28, 2026 per TxDMV. Local regulation remains barred. Authorization is a state permit, not a service area.
oversight: TxDMV commercial authorization; traffic-law and insurance requirements.

name: Utah
analysis: Utah Code Title 41 ch. 26 allows Level 3 vehicles under traffic-law and registration conditions and Level 4–5 vehicles to run driverless if they follow traffic law, meet federal standards and can reach a minimal risk condition. The system is the operator, owners must register and insure the vehicle, and localities cannot add AV-specific requirements.
oversight: State AV statute and ordinary traffic requirements.

name: Vermont
analysis: Vermont's Automated Vehicle Testing Act (23 V.S.A. ch. 41) covers testing only: testers need a Traffic Committee permit after a public hearing, an operator ready to take control, and at least $5 million in coverage. It is not a driverless passenger-service pathway.
oversight: Test-specific approval and public-comment process.

name: Virginia
analysis: Virginia considered autonomous operation licenses in SB 670, but the measure was continued to 2027 in the survey. Its proposed licenses are not existing permits.
oversight: General vehicle law pending any enacted AV-specific licensing framework.
source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

name: Washington
analysis: Washington regulates AV testing through Executive Order 17-02 and Department of Licensing self-certification rather than a statute. Companies need proof of insurance and an umbrella policy of at least $5,000,000 per occurrence and must file an annual collision report; self-certification is separate from vehicle registration.
oversight: State testing self-certification and vehicle registration processes.

name: West Virginia
analysis: West Virginia's Fully Autonomous Vehicle Act (W. Va. Code ch. 17H) allows driverless operation when the system is engaged, can reach a minimal risk condition, follows traffic law and bears federal certification labels, and covers commercial vehicles and on-demand networks. The Department of Transportation is the sole implementing agency and local AV-specific rules are barred.
oversight: State vehicle rules and law-enforcement interaction plan.
source_label: West Virginia Fully Autonomous Vehicle Act

name: Wisconsin
analysis: Wisconsin's AV steering committee addressed testing and deployment policy. Proposed 2026 board and permit legislation failed, leaving no such new permit in force.
oversight: General vehicle rules and existing agency coordination.
source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

name: Wyoming
analysis: The 2026 guide identifies no AV-specific operating law or new proposal in Wyoming. That finding does not amount to a positive authorization for any proposed service.
oversight: General motor vehicle and commercial-carrier rules.
source_label: State law survey (secondary source; verify primary text)

name: District of Columbia
analysis: D.C. allows only testing of vehicles with automated driving systems: testing needs an operator behind the wheel ready to take over, 10 business days' notice to DDOT and crash reporting. A testing allowance is not authorization for commercial deployment.
oversight: DDOT oversight.
source_label: DDOT AV law and testing guidance
